title: Polylogarithmic-query pattern-freeness testing
formal: For every integer \(k\ge2\) and every permutation \(\pi\) of \([k]\), is there a uniform randomized one-sided-error value-query tester \(A_\pi\) such that, for each fixed rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), there are integers \(C_{\pi,\varepsilon},a_{\pi,\varepsilon}\ge1\) for which the tester uses at most \[C_{\pi,\varepsilon}\bigl(1+\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil\bigr)^{a_{\pi,\varepsilon}}\] queries on every execution for every \(n\ge1\)? On input \(n,\varepsilon\) and access to any \(f:[n]\to\mathbb R\), it must accept with probability one if \(f\) is \(\pi\)-free, and reject with probability at least \(2/3\) if the normalized Hamming distance to \(\pi\)-freeness is at least \(\varepsilon\). No polynomial dependence on \(k\) or \(1/\varepsilon\) is required; those parameters are fixed when measuring the growth in \(n\).

source_formulation.text: We conjecture, however, that the query complexity is \(\operatorname{polylog} n\) for all constant \(k\).
source_formulation.caption: Selected source sentence; ICALP 2022 p. 98:5, mathematical typography normalized

why: A fixed order pattern is a basic obstruction in sequences and generalizes monotonicity. The conjecture asks whether adaptive access makes every such obstruction testable from only a polylogarithmic number of values, despite large lower bounds for predetermined queries. Its resolution would clarify the reach of adaptivity in ordered property testing and its connection with sublinear sequence analysis.
status_note: Source-open. On 15 September 2026, the full ICALP 2022 and final TheoretiCS 2024 formulations and the SODA 2026 hypergrid paper were checked. The latter explicitly retains the one-dimensional conjecture and separates it from its higher-dimensional obstruction. A bounded later-work search did not verify a resolution. The exact-real computation convention is an explicit model specification; cited proofs were not independently verified or formalized in Lean.

progress.text: ICALP publishes the general one-sided adaptive bound \(\widetilde O_{k,\varepsilon}(n^{O(1/\log\log\log n)})\) in Theorem 1.1, with the asymptotic understood for sufficiently large \(n\). Its open-question passage explicitly conjectures polylogarithmic complexity.
The final TheoretiCS paper retains the general subpolynomial upper bound and the explicit polylogarithmic conjecture on pp. 7–8.

The SODA hypergrid work distinguishes the unresolved conjecture for the line from a false analogous conjecture in dimension two. Its Introduction still identifies the Newman–Varma subpolynomial tester as the best general one-dimensional upper bound.

importance.reason: A uniform structural question over all fixed permutation patterns, with a major adaptive versus nonadaptive gap and links to monotonicity and sequence estimation. The first difficult nonmonotone patterns already have length four; the target goes beyond optimizing one tester.

sentences: A permutation pattern specifies the strict relative order of values at increasing positions of a real-valued sequence.
The question asks whether every fixed pattern has an adaptive one-sided tester using only a polylogarithmic number of queries in the sequence length.
Distance is the fraction of entries that must change to remove all occurrences, and the query bound may depend arbitrarily on the fixed pattern and proximity.
The checked general adaptive upper bound is subpolynomial but not polylogarithmic, while newer lower bounds on hypergrids concern a different domain.
Resolving the conjecture would clarify how much adaptive observations can improve the testing of ordered obstructions.

definitions: For a positive integer \(m\), write \([m]=\{1,\ldots,m\}\). A permutation \(\pi:[k]\to[k]\) is a bijection. A \(\pi\)-appearance in \(f:[n]\to\mathbb R\) consists of indices \(1\le i_1<\cdots<i_k\le n\) satisfying \[f(i_s)<f(i_t)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\pi(s)<\pi(t)\qquad(s,t\in[k]).\] The comparisons are strict, so all values in an appearance are distinct. The function is \(\pi\)-free if it has no such appearance. Inputs may have repeated values, and there is no monotonicity, bounded-range, integrality or permutation promise on \(f\). Let \(\mathcal F_{\pi,n}\) be all \(\pi\)-free real-valued functions on \([n]\), and define \[d_0(f,\mathcal F_{\pi,n})=\frac1n\min_{g\in\mathcal F_{\pi,n}}|\{i\in[n]:f(i)\ne g(i)\}|.\] For \(k\ge2\), the class is nonempty because a constant function is free, and a minimum exists among finitely many possible disagreement counts. When \(n<k\), every input is free. A query chooses an index \(i\) and returns the exact value \(f(i)\); every such call costs one. Queries may adapt to all earlier returned values and random bits. The tester is one finite program for the fixed \(\pi\), receiving \(n\) in binary and \(\varepsilon\) as a ratio of positive binary integers. Its work storage consists of integers, bit strings and exact real registers, with rational constants, copying, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by nonzero values, and exact equality and order comparisons. It uses independent fair random bits, has no real advice or other oracle, and must terminate on every execution. There is no cost bound on local computation or storage. This specifies the exact-value oracle model, not a bit-time or noisy-value model. The stated query bound is a worst-case bound over input functions and all random executions. Probabilities are over the program's random bits for a fixed function. Behavior at positive distance below \(\varepsilon\) is unrestricted. The program may depend on \(\pi\), and both the multiplicative constant and logarithmic exponent may also depend on the fixed \(\varepsilon\); neither may depend on \(n\) or \(f\).
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition or its logical negation with a complete Lean-checked proof. A positive answer must work for every fixed permutation pattern, arbitrary real-valued input functions and every positive rational proximity parameter, with one tester per pattern and the stated polylogarithmic-in-\(n\) worst-case query bound. A negative answer must rule out this guarantee for at least one pattern. A bound of \(n^{o(1)}\), a lower bound restricted to nonadaptive algorithms, or a result on a higher-dimensional domain does not settle this proposition.

context_blocks.text: A pattern specifies relative ranks rather than prescribed values. For example, \(\pi=(1,3,2)\) occurs at increasing positions when the first value is smallest, the second largest and the third between them. Equal values cannot form this occurrence. Avoiding \((2,1)\) is exactly being nondecreasing.

The repair distance counts how many entries must be changed, independently of how far their numerical values move. It is different from distances on permutations that charge the movement of points or inversions. Restricting the input itself to be a permutation would also change the model.

The source studies fixed pattern length and fixed proximity. This card therefore allows arbitrary dependence on those parameters and asks only for a polylogarithmic bound in sequence length. The one-sided convention follows the source algorithms and its separate discussion of whether two-sided error can help.

An adaptive tester can use values already seen to decide which positions to inspect next. A nonadaptive tester must select all query positions without their answers. The paper’s strongly sublinear adaptive bound and the much larger known worst-pattern nonadaptive bounds expose the importance of this distinction.

The best general bound in the checked source is \(\widetilde O_{k,\varepsilon}(n^{o(1)})\). A subpolynomial function of \(n\) can still grow faster than every fixed power of \(\log n\), so this does not establish the conjecture. The source separately records polylogarithmic bounds for patterns of length at most three and stronger bounds for monotone patterns.

The SODA 2026 hypergrid paper explicitly restates the one-dimensional conjecture. Its new polynomial lower bound concerns nonmonotone patterns on a two-dimensional partially ordered domain, where positions are not all comparable. It does not refute the conjecture on the line considered here.
